claims.text: An ML-enhanced thermodynamic-integration method can substantially reduce the cost of calculating fusion and high-temperature thermodynamic properties.
A sparsely trained ML interatomic potential can retain the accuracy needed to capture vibrational, anharmonic, and electron–vibration contributions.
The proposed initial domain is elemental and binary systems in solid and liquid phases near melting.
The ML potential will be trained on a strategically sparse set of high-fidelity ab initio free-energy data.
The trained ML potential will be incorporated into a thermodynamic-integration framework.
The method will be tested from approximately 0.8 to 1.2 times the experimental melting temperature.
Extension to multicomponent high-entropy alloys is deferred until after testing on elemental and binary systems.
The ML surrogate can reproduce an ab initio energy landscape accurately.
The surrogate will reproduce the structural fluctuations relevant to both solid and liquid states.
The surrogate will reproduce the entropy contributions needed for fusion free energies.
Interpolation of sparse ab initio data will capture the solid- and liquid-phase free-energy surfaces, including vibrational and anharmonic effects.
Using the ML potential in thermodynamic integration will greatly reduce the number of costly ab initio force evaluations.
Predicted free energies and fusion properties will agree with full ab initio molecular dynamics and TOR-TILD within 5–10%.
The method will provide roughly a tenfold computational speedup.
Explicit ab initio molecular dynamics and TOR-TILD provide benchmark phase free energies, melting temperatures, and associated entropy contributions.
The method's performance for highly multicomponent high-entropy alloys remains unestablished.
A decisive benchmark will compare solid- and liquid-phase free-energy curves from the ML method against full ab initio molecular dynamics or TOR-TILD over the same temperature range.
The hypothesis is falsified if phase free energies differ from the benchmark by more than 10%.
The hypothesis is falsified if the predicted melting temperature differs from the benchmark by more than 10%.
